passage: The storm knocked out the power across Chennai, and Keerthana's phone was on four per cent. Her younger brother Tejas, twenty, suddenly clutched his chest on the sofa, gasping. "I can't breathe. Something's wrong. Akka, I'm dying." Keerthana's own heart jumped into her throat. For a second she wanted to scream. Instead she lit a candle, sat beside him and kept her voice low and slow. "I'm here. This is panic. It's horrible, and it will pass. Breathe out with me, long." She didn't rush him or argue. Rain hammered the windows. After some minutes his breathing eased and he slumped against her, shaking. The next morning, she went with him to the doctor, and they asked about seeing a counsellor too.

qa.q: How much charge did Keerthana's phone have?
qa.a: It was on four per cent.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel when Tejas started gasping?
qa.a: She was frightened, her own heart jumping, and for a second she wanted to scream.

qa.q: What did Keerthana do that gave Tejas an anchor?
qa.a: She stayed steady and kind, lit a candle, sat close, spoke slowly and breathed with him, then took him to the doctor the next morning.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt when Keerthana stayed calm beside him?
qa.a: He may have felt safer and less alone, which helped him slump against her as the panic eased.

grounding: Shows a sister who feels scared seeing her brother gasping in panic, stays steady and kind as his anchor, and follows up with care, despite a storm and power cut.

passage: At the dinner table in their Kolkata flat, Bidisha, twenty, dropped her spoon and grabbed the table edge. Her breath came in short gasps. "Baba, my heart, I can't..." He pulled his chair next to hers and put his hand flat on the table near hers, not grabbing. "I'm right here, Bidisha. Look at me. Slow breath out." His voice shook only a little. He didn't fire questions at her. Slowly her grip loosened. Later, alone on the balcony, Ramesh let his own hands tremble. The next day he booked an appointment with their family doctor and went with her.

"Vaibhav? Vaibhav, what's happening?"
"Can't breathe. Imran, I think I'm dying."
"Okay. I'm here. I'm sitting right next to you." Imran's hands were shaking. He sat on the floor by the bed. "I think this is panic. It feels awful, but it passes. I'm not going anywhere."
"What if it doesn't stop?"
"It will. Breathe out slow. Like blowing out a candle. With me."
A long silence, just breathing.
"It's easing."
"Good. Good." Imran let out his own breath. "Honestly, you scared me."
"Sorry."
"Don't be sorry. But tomorrow, health centre. I'll come with you."
"Okay."

qa.a: He was scared, his hands shaking, though he kept his voice steady.

Then Hemant cried and tapped even more. One evening Manoj found him scrubbing at the sink, sobbing. He turned off the tap gently. "You're not naughty. This is scary for you, isn't it?" Hemant nodded. The next week they sat in a child psychologist's office, and she said, "We'll learn together how to boss that worry voice back."

"Papa, did you check the gas?"

"Beta, what happens if you don't?"
"Something bad happens to Mumma at her night shift." Her voice cracked. "I know it's silly. I can't stop."
Divyansh sat on the kitchen floor beside her. "It's not silly, and you're not in trouble. It's a worry that got too bossy."
"Will it go away?"
"On Thursday we're seeing Dr Meenakshi. She helps kids with worry loops like this. We'll learn together."
Ira leaned against him. "Okay. One more check tonight?"
"One more, then bed."

She explained that worry can make up rules, and that I could practise breaking them slowly. The first time I walked eleven steps, my heart pounded. Nani was fine. I still count sometimes, but it doesn't boss me like before.

She did all of it out of love, and she was exhausted. But the questions kept growing. At the district hospital, the child psychologist listened and said gently, "Your answers calm her for a minute, and then the worry wants more. Let's practise answering once, kindly, and then helping her wait." Nikita felt guilty, then hopeful.

passage: In their Toronto kitchen, Tariq rinsed the plates a third time, the way his son Paulo, ten, needed: hot water, left to right, no towel. Paulo watched from the doorway. If Tariq did it wrong, Paulo cried for an hour. So the whole family had changed: nobody touched Paulo's school bag, dinner started only after he checked the chairs. Tariq loved him fiercely and wanted him calm. But the rules kept multiplying. At the clinic, the psychologist explained, "When the family follows the rules, the fear learns it was right. We'll make a plan to step back slowly, together." Driving home, Tariq felt both relieved and afraid. That night he rinsed the plates once, and sat with Paulo while he cried.

"We do it so he won't be scared." The psychologist nodded. "You clearly love him. But each time you do it, the worry grows a bit stronger. I'll show you how to cut back gently, step by step." passage: At fifteen I thought I was a monster. I'm Pranav. It started in the temple: while everyone sang, a horrible thought flashed into my head, words I'd never say. So I stopped going to temple, stopped holding her, and told nobody. After months, I finally told Seema Ma'am, the school counsellor, shaking. She said, "Thoughts like these are really common. The fact that you hate them shows who you are." She helped me see a psychologist. Slowly, the thoughts lost their grip. I held my cousin again last Diwali.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 10, Monday.
Tanvir came in after asking twice to "talk about something bad." He could barely look at me. He said that for months he's had sudden thoughts he hates, of shouting something cruel at his mother or of hurting his dog. He has never acted on them and is horrified by them. He has been avoiding his dog and cries at night, sure it means he is evil.
I told him these kinds of thoughts are common, that they are not wishes, and that his distress shows how much he cares. With his agreement, I phoned his parents during the session and recommended a clinical psychologist, who can help with this. He left looking lighter. Next: check in Thursday. — Usha

Sunday
At the gurdwara today, in the middle of kirtan, an awful thought came into my head. The kind I'd never, ever say. I felt sick and ran out to the shoe area. Why does my brain do this? It keeps happening. I'm scared I'm a bad person underneath.
I've never told anyone because they'd look at me differently.
But tonight Kishore Mama saw me crying on the stairs and sat down. I told him a little bit. He didn't look shocked at all. He said lots of people get thoughts they hate, and it doesn't mean anything about who you are. He said the shame is what keeps them loud. He's talking to Mum tonight about a psychologist.
I feel a bit lighter.
Jasleen

Dear Ramesh bhaiya,
You asked why I missed your engagement lunch. I owe you the truth.
Every morning I spend nearly two hours checking the stove, the lock, the window latches, the plugs. Then I arrange my books by height and colour, and if one is wrong I start again. I've been late to lectures most of this term. I told my friends I had a stomach problem. They believe me.
The strange thing is, checking calms me for maybe a minute. Then the fear comes back bigger, and I need to check more.
I don't want to live like this. So yesterday I booked an appointment with a clinical psychologist at the university health centre. It's on Tuesday.
I'm sorry about the lunch. I really wanted to be there.
Abhinav

passage: "Mohit, you jump every time it thunders, na? Let me tell you about myself. When I was nine, the river flooded our village at night. We climbed onto the roof in the rain. My Abba didn't scold. He made the same evening routine every day: dinner, one story, lamp on. And he took me to a doctor in the town who knew about children and frightening things. passage: "Varun, you pushed your friend yesterday and then hated yourself for it, na? Sit. When I was fifteen, there was a robbery in our house at night. passage: In his classroom in Nairobi, Ivan saw Wanjiru, fourteen, explode when a boy scraped his chair loudly behind her. She swept her books off the desk and shouted. Last week she had gone silent for a whole lesson after a door slammed. Ivan didn't send her out or scold her in front of everyone. After class, he asked quietly, "Something happened that made that noise hard. Do you want to tell me what happened?" She stared at the floor. "There was a crash near our house. I still hear it."
